title: Kings of the North and the South
sum: The long speech that began in chapter 10 now runs through two centuries. A heavenly messenger tells Daniel what is written in the "writing of truth": the last kings of Persia, a mighty king of Greece whose empire breaks in four, and then, for most of the chapter, the wars between two of its pieces. The king of the south rules Egypt and the king of the north rules Syria. The Beautiful Land lies between them and is passed back and forth (11:1-20).

From 11:21 the story narrows to one man, a "despicable" king who seizes power by smooth schemes, humiliates Egypt's army, is turned back by ships from Kittim, and then takes out his anger on the holy covenant. He ends the regular offering and sets up the abomination that desolates (11:21-31). The people who know their God resist; the teachers with insight instruct the many and are cut down, yet are refined by it (11:32-35). The chapter ends with a king who exalts himself above every god and meets his end "between the seas and the holy mountain of beauty" (11:36-45).
readings: Read as prophecy given in advance

On the traditional dating, Daniel received this speech in 536 BC, in the third year of Cyrus (10:1). It then foretold some 370 years of history, from Daniel's day to Antiochus IV, and ends with a king still to come. Defenders of the sixth-century date, among them E. J. Young and Gleason Archer, take the chapter as real prediction and as evidence that God knows the future. The angel's repeated "it is still for the time set" (11:27, 35) is the voice of a God who runs history to a schedule.
Read as history written as prophecy

On the critical dating, the book's final form comes from about 165 BC. The detail up to Antiochus' second Egyptian campaign and the profaning of the Temple (167 BC) is accurate because the author is describing events he knew. The vague and wrong parts, the end of Antiochus in 11:40-45 and the Persian kings in 11:2, are where his knowledge stopped. The point of the form is comfort: for people being killed, God's plan was fixed long before and has an end.

Many Jewish and Christian readers have kept the history and also looked past it. Antiochus becomes the type of a final tyrant, so the same words describe a king in each age. Jerome reports that Christians read 11:36-45 of the Antichrist while Porphyry read all of it of Antiochus; Rashi reads it of Rome.

views.H: This chapter is the best test of history and fulfillment in the book. 11:3-35 can be matched with Alexander, the Ptolemies and Seleucids, Rome's arrival, and the persecution of 167-164 BC, using Polybius, Josephus and 1-2 Maccabees. Defenders of the sixth-century date read it as prophecy fulfilled; those who date the book to the 160s BC read it as history. Both note that 11:40-45 does not match Antiochus' death in Persia in 164 BC.
views.C: Critical scholars (Collins and others) say the chapter is one of the strongest signs of a Maccabean date: the survey becomes detailed and exact as it approaches 167 BC, then loses its footing. Porphyry made this argument in the third century and Jerome answered it. The vague Persian history (11:2), the ending that misses (11:40-45), and the point of view of the teachers (11:33-35) all fit a book finished about 165-164 BC.
views.J: Jewish tradition keeps the Greek-period history but adds Rome. Rashi reads the "Kittim" of 11:30 as Romans and the king of 11:36 as the kingdom of Rome. The events of 167-164 BC are remembered at Hanukkah (the topic page), whose rabbinic liturgy and story do not mention Daniel. The Talmud lists Daniel among the Writings (Bava Batra 14b), and its warning against counting the end (Sanhedrin 97b) shadows the readers of chapters 11-12.
views.X: Hippolytus (about AD 200) already read the Antichrist in Daniel's visions, and later fathers read 11:36-45 of him. Porphyry (died about AD 305) replied that the whole chapter described Antiochus IV. Jerome (AD 407) reports both readings and takes Antiochus as the type of the Antichrist. Jesus' mention of "the abomination of desolation" (Matthew 24:15) pointed Christians back to 11:31. Reformation churches heard the Antichrist in the pope (the Smalcald Articles, the Westminster Confession), while Catholic writers such as Bellarmine looked for him in the future.
views.F: Futurist readers (dispensational and others) stop the history at 11:35 or 11:39 and read 11:36-45 as a final world ruler and his campaigns at the end of the age, with the "time of the end" in 11:40 a real end. Jewish hope also places a last battle of the nations in the land (Ezekiel 38-39). Critics object that 11:41 names Edom, Moab and Ammon, nations that have long since disappeared; futurists reply that the names mark the region east of the Jordan, which they identify with modern Jordan.

deep.h: Who is who: the kings of chapter 11
deep.b:
These are the identifications most scholars (Collins, Goldingay) give, with Jerome's account where he differs. The Hebrew never uses a name.

  • 11:2 Persian kings: Cambyses, Bardiya (or Smerdis), Darius I, Xerxes I (486-465 BC).
  • 11:3-4 Alexander the Great (died 323 BC) and his divided empire.
  • 11:5 Ptolemy I Soter of Egypt and Seleucus I Nicator of Syria (died 282/281 BC).
  • 11:6 Berenice, daughter of Ptolemy II, marries Antiochus II about 252 BC; murdered 246 BC.
  • 11:7-9 Ptolemy III Euergetes invades Syria (246-241 BC); Seleucus II's counter-attack (about 242 BC) fails.
  • 11:10-12 Antiochus III the Great (223-187 BC) is beaten by Ptolemy IV at Raphia (217 BC).
  • 11:13-16 Antiochus III defeats Egypt at Panium and Sidon (200-198 BC) and takes the Beautiful Land.
  • 11:17 His daughter Cleopatra I is given to Ptolemy V (about 193 BC).
  • 11:18-19 Scipio checks him at Magnesia (190 BC); he dies at Elymais in 187 BC.
  • 11:20 Seleucus IV (187-175 BC) and his minister Heliodorus.
  • 11:21-35 Antiochus IV Epiphanes (175-164 BC): rise, two Egyptian campaigns (170 and 168 BC), the Roman envoy at Eleusis (168 BC), the profaning of the Temple (167 BC), the faithful teachers.
  • 11:36-45 A king who exalts himself: Antiochus IV in the critical reading; the Antichrist, Rome or a later power in others.

Up to 11:35 the match with known events is close. From 11:36 the text talks of a king who "does as he likes", honors a god of fortresses, conquers Egypt, and then meets an end "between the seas and the holy mountain of beauty." Antiochus IV never conquered Egypt after Eleusis (168 BC). He died in Persia in 164 BC after failing to plunder a temple there (1 Maccabees 6:1-16; 2 Maccabees 9). So there are three main ways to read the break. (1) The author, writing about 165 BC, expected the king to fall in Judea and was wrong in detail (Collins). (2) The verses are about a later figure; Jerome says Christians say the Antichrist, and futurists agree. (3) The verses describe what Antiochus did and will do in language that is symbolic and does not map onto known events (some conservative scholars).

A fourth line is that the author had real but now lost information about a last campaign of Antiochus. Nothing in the surviving sources shows this.

The witnesses used for chapters 11-12 are the Leningrad Codex (the site's word-by-word Hebrew), the Abegg-Bowley-Cook transcription of the Dead Sea Scrolls through the site's tool (4QDan-a, 4Q112; 4QDan-c, 4Q114; 6QpapDan, 6Q7), the Old Greek in Swete's edition (Codex Chisianus), and Theodotion's Greek. The manuscripts themselves, Papyrus 967 and Ziegler's Göttingen edition were not consulted; statements about them follow the literature. In chapter 11 the scrolls preserve parts of 11:1-2 (4Q114), 11:13-16 (4Q112), 11:13-17 and 11:25-29 (4Q114) and 11:33-38 (6Q7). They agree with the Masoretic Text except for spelling and the differences listed in the variants (11:1, 11:16, 11:17). No scroll in the transcription preserves chapter 12.

echoes: Daniel 7:8, 24-25; Daniel 8:9-14, 21-25; Daniel 9:26-27; Daniel 10:20-21; Numbers 24:24; Isaiah 8:7-8; Isaiah 14:13-14; Isaiah 23:1; Ezekiel 28:2; Ezekiel 38:1-23; 1 Maccabees 1:1-64; 1 Maccabees 6:1-16; 2 Maccabees 4-6; 2 Maccabees 9; Matthew 24:15; Mark 13:14; 2 Thessalonians 2:3-4; Revelation 13:5-6; Revelation 19:19-21

settings.what: The angel's survey of Persia, Greece and the Ptolemies and Seleucids
settings.by: The heavenly messenger who has spoken with Daniel since 10:10, from "the writing of truth" (10:21)
settings.to: Daniel by the Tigris, in the third year of Cyrus (10:1; about 536 BC)
settings.when: after three weeks of mourning and prayer, when the messenger has returned from the fight with the prince of Persia (10:12-20)
settings.why: To answer Daniel's concern for his people (10:14): they will live under a succession of foreign kings, and each rise and fall is known. The listing of empires gives the oppressed a calendar of God's control.
settings.readers: Readers in the 160s BC (the critical view) knew every name behind the "king of the south" and "king of the north", since Egypt and Syria were their rulers. The long survey shows that their present suffering is the end of a story that was always going to be told.
views: The speech was given to Daniel in 536 BC and its readers in the exile and Persian period received it as a sealed prophecy; its meaning was clear only as events unfolded.
The author uses Daniel's name for a survey of events up to his own day, and the first hearers are the people of Judea in 167-164 BC, who could check it against what they had lived through.

settings.what: The rise of the despicable king and the persecution of the faithful
settings.to: Daniel (inside the story); the "teachers with insight" of 11:33 and the "many" they instruct (for the readers)
settings.when: in the vision, in Persia 536 BC; for the Maccabean readers, 167-164 BC while the persecution is under way
settings.why: To tell the faithful what to expect and how to behave: do not give in (11:32), instruct the people (11:33), take the little help that comes without trusting it (11:34), and understand that being cut down is part of the refining (11:35). It is the only part of the book that addresses a way of life under persecution.
settings.readers: For readers under Antiochus IV it names their own king, their own Temple, their own martyrs. For later Jews and Christians it is a pattern for any persecution.
views: The "teachers with insight" are the writers and first readers of the book; 11:33-35 is its author's self-portrait.
Daniel foresees a future group of faithful teachers whom the angel calls to courage; the account of Antiochus is real prophecy, and the same group may be Daniel's own.

settings.what: The king who exalts himself and his end
settings.to: Daniel and, through him, those living in "the time of the end" (11:40; 12:4, 9)
settings.when: set at the time of the end; read by Maccabean readers in 165-164 BC, by the early church in the age of the persecutions, and by the Reformation churches against Rome
settings.why: To show that the persecutor's arrogance has a limit. He speaks "shocking things" against the God of gods, but only "until the fury is finished." Telling the end of the tyrant in advance is meant to keep the faithful from despair.
settings.readers: If the book was written about 165 BC, the first readers would have understood the tyrant as Antiochus. Later readers made him the Antichrist (so the early church), the Roman power (so Rashi), or a final world ruler (so futurist readers).
views: Porphyry, Collins and most critical scholars: the king is Antiochus, and the unmatched ending is a failed prediction or a literary pattern.
The Antichrist or a later power
Jerome's report of the church's reading, the dispensationalists (Pentecost) and many others: the chapter turns to a future figure at 11:36 or 11:40.
Rashi on 11:36: the kingdom of Rome.

traditions.q: Who is the king who exalts himself in Daniel 11:36-45, and is he the Antichrist?
views: The Catechism speaks of a final trial before Christ's return and says "the supreme religious deception is that of the Antichrist" (Catechism 675). It does not tie Daniel 11:36-45 to a named person. Jerome (AD 407), whose commentary shaped Catholic reading, takes the passage as the Antichrist with Antiochus as his type. Augustine (City of God 20.19) expects a final Antichrist and, as an amillennial reader, sets his coming at the end of the age.

The Orthodox teaching rests on the fathers, who expect one future Antichrist. Hippolytus (about AD 200, On Christ and Antichrist) and Cyril of Jerusalem (Catechetical Lectures 15) draw him from Daniel's beast and horn visions and from 2 Thessalonians 2. These fathers name him as a single man and do not name the pope.

The Smalcald Articles (1537), a Lutheran confession, call the pope "the very Antichrist" (Part II, Article IV). The article is about the pope's claim to rule the Church; it does not comment on Daniel 11:36-45.

The Westminster Confession of Faith 25.6 (1646) says the pope of Rome "is that Antichrist, that man of sin, and son of perdition" who exalts himself against Christ. It does not mention Daniel 11. (The American revision of 1788 removed this sentence.)
The Second London Confession 26.4 (1689) repeats the Westminster statement about the pope as the Antichrist. Later Baptist statements such as the Baptist Faith and Message (2000) do not repeat it.
The king of 11:36 and following is the future Antichrist, a Gentile ruler of the end-time tribulation, who is a single person and not an institution (Pentecost, Things to Come).

title: Some to Everlasting Life
sum: The messenger's speech reaches its goal. At the time of the king's end, Michael the great prince will stand up, a time of distress such as the nation has never known will come, and everyone found written in the scroll will escape (12:1). Then comes the clearest promise of resurrection in the Hebrew Bible: many who sleep in the dusty ground will wake, some to life without end and some to shame (12:2). Those with insight will gleam like the sky, and those who put the many in the right will blaze like the stars (12:3).

Daniel is told to keep the words secret and seal the scroll (12:4). In a last vision two others stand on the banks of the river and one of them asks the man in linen clothes, "How long?" He swears by the one who lives forever that it will be a time, times and half a time (12:5-7). Daniel does not understand, and is given two more numbers, 1,290 and 1,335 days, and a blessing for the one who waits (12:8-12). The book ends with a promise to Daniel himself: he will rest, and he will rise to his share at the end of the days (12:13).
readings: Read as the resurrection of the dead

Most Jewish and Christian readers have heard 12:2 as bodily resurrection at the end of the age. The Pharisees held it (Josephus, Antiquities 18.14), the Mishnah makes it a test of faith, and Jesus and Paul speak of a resurrection of the righteous and the unrighteous (John 5:28-29; Acts 24:15). On this reading 12:3 promises the faithful a place of brightness beside the angels.
Read as the martyrs of the persecution

Others, including Collins and Nickelsburg, think "many" means not all the dead, but the exceptionally righteous who died under Antiochus and the exceptionally wicked who betrayed them. It answers a question of the persecution: what of those who die for the covenant (11:33-35)? It is the comfort the book offers its first readers.

A few critics have read 12:2 as a figure for Israel's recovery, as in Ezekiel's valley of dry bones (Ezekiel 37). The text speaks of individuals who wake to different fates, so this reading is hard to hold alone.

views.H: In the sixth-century reading, the time of distress is Antiochus' persecution or the final tribulation. In the Maccabean reading, 12:1-3 is the hope offered to the martyrs of 167-164 BC. Either way, 12:1 is the book's last word about history: God's side wins.
views.C: Critical scholars see 12:1-3 as the center of the book's message: resurrection and angelic glory for those who die faithful, one of the earliest and clearest texts of the afterlife. They read the numbers in 12:7-12 as successive corrections of the date of the end that did not arrive (Collins), and 12:4, 9 as the author's way of explaining why an old prophet's book appeared only now.
views.J: The rabbis take 12:2 as the resurrection of the dead (Rashi: "The dead will come to life"); the Mishnah says a person who denies that the Torah teaches the resurrection loses a share in the world to come (Sanhedrin 10:1). Michael is the guardian of Israel. The Talmud warns against computing the end (Sanhedrin 97b), a warning aimed at readers of 12:11-12. Daniel's "rest" at 12:13 became the model of the righteous dead who wait.
views.X: The New Testament builds on 12:1-3 more than on almost any other Old Testament passage: Matthew 24:21 and Mark 13:19 (the unmatched distress), John 5:28-29 and Acts 24:15 (the two resurrections), Matthew 13:43 (the righteous shining), Revelation 7:14, 10:5-6 and 12:7 (the great suffering, the oath, Michael). The church read the "book" as the book of life (Revelation 20:12-15) and 12:2 as the resurrection at Christ's return.
views.F: Futurist readers place 12:1 at the middle or end of the seven-year tribulation, 12:2 at its end (the resurrection of Old Testament saints and tribulation martyrs, in dispensational teaching), and read the 1,290 and 1,335 days as literal days after the midpoint. Historicists count the days as years. Jewish hope sees 12:1-3 as the days of the Messiah and the world to come.

deep.h: How the hope of resurrection grew
deep.b:
The Hebrew Bible knows death as a descent to Sheol, from which no one returns (Job 7:9; Psalm 88:10-12). Hints of more appear in Psalm 16:10, Psalm 49:15, Hosea 6:2, Isaiah 25:8 and Isaiah 26:19, and Ezekiel 37 pictures a nation brought back from death. Daniel 12:2 is the first text most scholars agree speaks of individuals waking to different fates. 2 Maccabees 7 shows the hope at work: the seven brothers say as they die that the King of the universe will raise them (2 Maccabees 7:9, 14). The Pharisees held it and the Sadducees did not (Josephus, War 2.162-166). The New Testament assumes it.

Daniel 12 says two things at once: some wake to life, some to shame. That makes the resurrection also a judgment, the way Isaiah 66:24 ends with the corpses of rebels. How long the second fate lasts is the main difference between the churches (see the card below).

Revelation reworks Daniel 12 more than any other chapter. The angel who swears with his hand raised by the one who lives forever (Revelation 10:5-6) takes the oath of Daniel 12:7; the "time, and times, and half a time" of Revelation 12:14 is Daniel's; the "great suffering" of Revelation 7:14 echoes Daniel 12:1; the book of life (Revelation 3:5; 20:12) is Daniel's scroll; and Michael fights the dragon in Revelation 12:7. Where Daniel is told to seal the scroll (12:4), John is told not to (Revelation 22:10): the time that Daniel's book looked forward to has come near.

See the note at 12:11. In brief: 1,260 is three and a half years of 360 days; 1,290 adds thirty days; 1,335 adds another forty-five. The numbers are a puzzle for every reading. Jewish tradition (Sanhedrin 97b) warned against calculating. Jerome (AD 407) reads the 1,290 days as the Antichrist's persecution, which he gives as three and a half years or 1,290 days, and the extra 45 as a further wait that tests the saints' patience, for a reason known to God. Porphyry, as Jerome reports him, tied the numbers to Antiochus and the Maccabean victory. Critical scholars (Collins) read the added numbers as later adjustments when the end did not come as first expected.

echoes: Genesis 3:19; Daniel 7:10; Daniel 7:25-27; Daniel 9:26-27; Job 38:7; Isaiah 4:3; Isaiah 26:19; Isaiah 52:13; Isaiah 53:10-12; Isaiah 66:24; Jeremiah 30:7; Ezekiel 9:2-11; Ezekiel 37:1-14; Hosea 6:2; Joel 2:2; Zechariah 13:9; Malachi 3:16; Matthew 13:43; Matthew 24:21; Mark 13:19; John 5:28-29; Acts 24:15; 1 Thessalonians 4:13-17; Revelation 7:14; Revelation 10:5-6; Revelation 12:7; Revelation 12:14; Revelation 20:11-15; Revelation 22:10; Jude 9

settings.what: The promise of rescue, resurrection and shining, and the command to seal the book
settings.to: Daniel, and through him the faithful in the time of distress
settings.when: at the end of the long speech of chapters 11-12, set in 536 BC (10:1)
settings.why: To close the survey of kings with a hope bigger than the kings: Michael will stand up, the faithful will escape, the dead will wake, and the teachers who died will shine. The command to seal says the book is for a later time.
settings.readers: For readers in the 160s BC (the critical view) these verses answered the question raised by every martyrdom: what do those who die faithful get? For later Jewish and Christian readers they became a main text for the afterlife.
views: Daniel is told to seal the book because its meaning belongs to the time of the end, which is far off, and later readers will understand it.
The sealing is the author's way of setting the book in an older time; the "time of the end" is his own, and the unsealing is the book's appearance.

settings.what: The oath of the man in linen clothes, the numbers, and Daniel's own promise
settings.by: The man in linen clothes (12:6-7). Daniel calls the speaker "my lord" (12:8) and the reply in 12:9-13 comes from the same voice in the Hebrew; some readers think the heavenly messenger of chapters 10-11 takes over, and the Hebrew does not mark a change
settings.to: Daniel by the river; two angels who ask the question (12:5-6)
settings.when: on the bank of the Tigris, in the vision of Cyrus' third year (10:1, 4)
settings.why: To say how long, and to refuse a calendar of the end. The oath fixes a limit (a time, times and half a time), but Daniel does not understand, and the added numbers (1,290, 1,335) leave the answer open. The last verse turns from the people's future to Daniel's own: he is to go to his rest, and his place is kept.
settings.readers: For readers under Antiochus IV (critical view) the numbers marked the days they were counting, and the later numbers reflect extra waiting. For later readers the numbers have been a problem and an invitation, which is why Jewish tradition warned against using them.
views: The numbers are literal or symbolic periods of a real future persecution, and the book stays sealed until then.
The numbers are successive adjustments for the persecution of 167-164 BC, with the last blessing for those who stayed faithful to the end.

traditions.q: What does Daniel 12:2 teach about the resurrection, and about the fate of the wicked?
views: All the dead will rise, the righteous and the unrighteous alike (Acts 24:15), and the Last Judgment follows (Catechism 1038). Those who die in mortal sin face the punishment of hell, "eternal fire" (Catechism 1035).

The Church confesses "the resurrection of the dead and the life of the age to come" in the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed. The Confession of Dositheus (1672, Decree 18) teaches that the souls of the departed are at rest or in torment according to their lives, and that their state is completed at the resurrection of the body. The anathemas against Origen attached to the Fifth Council (553) condemn the teaching that the punishment of the wicked and of demons will one day end. Some Orthodox writers, Kallistos Ware among them, hope that all may be saved; Ware presents this as a hope and not as the Church's doctrine.

At the end Christ will raise all the dead, give eternal life to believers, and condemn the ungodly "to be tormented without end" (Augsburg Confession XVII). The Confession rejects the view that the punishment of the damned will end.
All the dead will be raised with the same bodies: the just to honor and the unjust to dishonor, and the wicked are cast into "eternal torments" (Westminster Confession 32.2-3; 33.2).
The Second London Confession (1689, chapters 31-32) follows the Westminster Confession: one resurrection of all, then the final judgment, with eternal punishment for the wicked.

Resurrection comes in stages: the church at the rapture, then Old Testament saints and tribulation martyrs after the tribulation (the usual dispensational reading of Daniel 12:2), and the wicked dead at the end of the thousand years (Pentecost, Things to Come).

The righteous dead are raised at Christ's return and the wicked after the thousand years; the wicked are then destroyed and cease to exist (Fundamental Beliefs 26 and 27). Adventists reject unending torment.

The dead are unconscious until raised. "Hell" is the common grave. Most of the dead will be raised to life on earth; the unrighteous may live again and be judged, and those who finally reject God are destroyed forever.

Most evangelicals teach unending conscious punishment. A minority hold conditional immortality: the wicked are raised, judged and finally destroyed (Edward Fudge, The Fire That Consumes; John Stott held it tentatively in Essentials).

traditions.q: Who is Michael, the great prince of Daniel 12:1?
views: Michael is an archangel, a created spiritual being (Catechism 328-330). The Church keeps the feast of the Archangels Michael, Gabriel and Raphael on 29 September (Catechism 335).
The chief of the angelic powers, an archangel. The Church keeps the Synaxis of the Archangel Michael and the other bodiless powers on 8 November.

The Reformed confessions say what angels are: creatures that God made good (Belgic Confession, article 12). They do not say who Michael is. Reformed commentators differ. Calvin, on 12:1, reports that many understand Michael as Christ, the head of the Church, and says that if the archangel seems better the sense still fits; he leaves both open (see the card at Daniel 10:13). Matthew Henry reads the "great prince" of 12:1 as Christ, the church's patron and protector.

The Fundamental Beliefs do not mention Michael. Adventist writers, following Ellen White, identify Michael with Christ and read 12:1 as Christ ending his work as mediator before the final time of trouble (The Great Controversy, chapter 39, "The Time of Trouble").
Michael is another name for Jesus Christ in his heavenly role, and 12:1 describes Christ taking up his rule.
